137.text:
Many illnesses, from heart disease to infections, could be avoided if people knew how to protect themselves. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on public health campaigns: improved health and behaviour, and lower costs and a stronger economy.

First and foremost, public health campaigns reach millions of people at a low cost per person. Television, social media, schools and posters can spread simple, repeated messages about smoking, handwashing, vaccination or diet, and well-known figures and real stories make the advice memorable. A campaign that shows the real story of a former smoker, for example, can persuade more people to quit than a list of statistics. As a result, habits change gradually, fewer people become ill, and the whole population becomes more aware of how to stay healthy. Campaigns also reduce stigma around subjects such as mental health and sexual health, which encourages people to seek help earlier.

In addition, public health campaigns lower costs and strengthen the economy. Preventing illness is cheaper than treating it, so every unit of money spent on prevention can save several times as much on hospitals and medicine. Healthy people take fewer sick days and work more productively, which supports economic growth. Countries that have run long campaigns against smoking have seen smoking rates fall and fewer people develop lung disease. Although campaigns do not work alone and need to be supported by services and rules, their wide reach makes them one of the most cost-effective tools available, and the results are likely to last for generations.

To sum up, public health campaigns bring clear benefits to a country, above all healthier behaviour and lower long-term costs. For these reasons, they deserve sustained public support.

359.text:
Many serious diseases are easier to treat if they are found early, and some countries run programmes to test large numbers of people before symptoms appear. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on early disease detection programmes: better survival and health, and savings for the health system and economy.

First and foremost, detecting disease early makes treatment simpler, cheaper and more successful. Screening for cancer, diabetes and heart disease finds problems before symptoms appear, when a small operation or medicine may be enough, whereas late discovery needs long and costly care. A woman whose breast cancer is found at a routine scan, for example, may need only a small operation and be back at work within weeks. As a result, more people survive, suffer less and keep their independence. Children can also be checked for hearing and vision problems, so that they receive help before they fall behind at school.

In addition, early detection brings savings and economic benefits. Treating advanced disease requires long hospital stays, expensive drugs and sometimes lifelong care, while early treatment costs much less. Healthy workers remain productive, and families are spared the loss of income and the emotional strain of serious illness. Although screening programmes require equipment, trained staff and public awareness, and sometimes produce false alarms, these costs are small compared with the benefits. Wider use of simple tests, such as blood pressure checks, can also be extended to rural areas through mobile services, so that everyone benefits and inequalities in health are reduced.

To sum up, early disease detection programmes bring clear benefits to a country, above all better survival and lower costs. For these reasons, they deserve sustained public support.

398.text:
Advertisements for soap, soft drinks and cars change what people buy, and governments hope that public health campaigns can change behaviour in the same way. This essay will explain two key ways in which public campaigns change health behaviours: by spreading simple messages widely and by changing what people see as normal.

First and foremost, public health campaigns reach millions of people at a low cost per person. Television, social media, schools and posters can spread simple, repeated messages about smoking, handwashing, vaccination or diet, and well-known figures and real stories make the advice memorable. A campaign that shows the real story of a former smoker, for example, can persuade more people to quit than a list of statistics. Messages that give a clear, easy action, such as washing hands for twenty seconds, are more likely to be remembered and followed than general warnings.

In addition, campaigns change social attitudes. When wearing a seat belt or avoiding smoking in public is shown as normal and responsible, people tend to follow the example of those around them, and young people learn what is expected. However, information alone does not change behaviour if people cannot act on it. People may know that vegetables are healthy but lack the money or time to buy them, and messages that lecture or frighten can be ignored. Campaigns therefore work best when combined with services, rules and prices that support the advice, such as free vaccination, taxes on tobacco or healthier school meals. Evaluating results and adjusting the message also improves success.

To sum up, public campaigns can change health behaviours by spreading memorable messages and shaping social norms, but they are most effective when supported by practical measures. For these reasons, they should be one part of a wider strategy.

324.text:
Stress, depression and burnout are among the leading reasons for absence from work, and many employees are afraid to admit that they are struggling. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on laws and standards for employers and on services and awareness.

To begin with, governments should require and encourage mentally healthy workplaces. Laws on working hours and workload, free counselling, training for managers, flexible hours and campaigns against stigma help employees to cope before stress becomes illness. An employee who is expected to answer emails late at night, for example, may develop anxiety long before anyone notices, so limits on out-of-hours contact can protect wellbeing. Employers could be required to assess psychological risks, just as they must assess physical hazards, and tax benefits or public recognition could reward companies that do this well. Small firms need advice and templates, since they rarely have specialist staff.

In addition, authorities should provide accessible services and promote awareness. Affordable counselling and helplines, available outside working hours, give employees somewhere to turn, and mental health first-aid training enables colleagues to recognise warning signs. Public campaigns that present mental illness as a health condition, not a weakness, make workers more willing to ask for help early. Equally important, support for people returning to work after illness, such as gradual return plans, prevents relapse. Such measures cost less than the loss of productivity and the sick pay that result from untreated problems, and they help to retain experienced staff.

In conclusion, setting clear workplace standards and providing accessible services and awareness campaigns offer the most realistic way of supporting mental health in the workplace.

445.text:
Painting, music, drama and dance are usually seen as leisure activities, but they are increasingly used by trained therapists to help people with mental health problems. This essay will outline two roles that arts therapy plays in treatment: giving patients a means of expression and supporting wellbeing alongside other treatments.

First and foremost, arts therapy gives people a way to express feelings that they cannot put into words. Painting, music and drama allow patients to explore painful experiences safely, reduce stress and build confidence, which helps those who find talking therapy difficult. A child who cannot speak about a frightening experience, for example, may be able to show it through drawing, and the therapist can then help the child to talk about it. People with dementia or autism, and survivors of trauma, may also respond to music or art when words fail. Creating something can give a sense of control and achievement to those who feel helpless.

In addition, arts therapy supports wellbeing alongside other treatments. Group sessions reduce loneliness by bringing people together, and the focus on creating something shifts attention away from worries and symptoms. Many hospitals now include art or music sessions in their care for conditions such as depression, anxiety and addiction. However, arts therapy is not a replacement for medication or counselling in serious illness, and evidence of its benefits, though encouraging, is still developing. It works best alongside, not instead of, other treatments, and it requires trained professionals so that patients are protected.

To sum up, arts therapy plays a valuable role in mental health treatment by offering a gentle way to express feelings and by supporting recovery. For these reasons, it deserves continued support.

296.text:
Unemployment, poverty, crime and family breakdown are often blamed on economic or political failure, but some argue that poor health is the main cause of social problems. I partly agree with this view, since illness can trigger a chain of difficulties, although it is not the only or even the main cause in every case.

To begin with, poor health can trigger a chain of social problems. Illness reduces the ability to work and earn, leads to debt and family stress, and may cause isolation or substance abuse. A father who falls ill and cannot work, for example, may plunge his family into debt and stress, and his children may miss out on education and opportunities. Mental illness that is untreated can also lead to homelessness, broken relationships and, in some cases, crime. In poorer countries, widespread disease holds back whole communities, since sick people cannot farm, study or run businesses.

However, poor health is rarely the only cause. Inequality, weak education and unemployment also create social problems independently, and they often cause poor health in the first place, so cause and effect run in both directions. A person who loses a job, for instance, may fall into poverty and then become ill because of stress, bad housing or poor diet. Social problems such as corruption, discrimination and lack of opportunity cannot be explained by health alone. Tackling them requires fair economic policies, good schools and strong institutions as well as health services. Health is therefore a major cause but part of a wider cycle.

In conclusion, poor health is an important cause of social problems, but it interacts with poverty, education and inequality, so I agree only partly that it is the main cause.

analysis.type_vi: Extent: sức khoẻ kém là nguyên nhân chính của vấn đề xã hội — đồng ý một phần

plan.step: 1. Khung Extent với lập trường 'một phần'
plan.think: Đề nêu 'main cause' nên đồng ý một phần là hợp lý: sức khoẻ kém là nguyên nhân quan trọng nhưng không phải duy nhất hay chính trong mọi trường hợp.

Bệnh làm giảm khả năng làm việc và kiếm tiền, dẫn đến nợ và căng thẳng gia đình, cô lập hay lạm dụng chất; bệnh tâm thần không điều trị dẫn đến vô gia cư, đổ vỡ quan hệ, đôi khi phạm tội; nước nghèo bệnh tật kìm hãm cả cộng đồng. Ví dụ người cha ốm không làm việc được đẩy gia đình vào nợ.

Bất bình đẳng, giáo dục yếu, thất nghiệp tự gây vấn đề xã hội và thường gây sức khoẻ kém từ đầu: nhân quả hai chiều. Ví dụ mất việc rồi nghèo rồi ốm vì căng thẳng, nhà ở tệ. Tham nhũng, phân biệt đối xử không giải thích bằng sức khoẻ; cần chính sách kinh tế công bằng, trường tốt, thể chế mạnh.
Sức khoẻ là nguyên nhân quan trọng nhưng tương tác với nghèo, giáo dục, bất bình đẳng; đồng ý một phần.

290.text:
Smog over cities, polluted rivers and chemicals in the soil are not only environmental issues but also health issues, and some argue that stricter environmental laws improve public health. I largely agree, although the benefits depend on enforcement and on other health measures.

To begin with, stricter environmental laws protect people from pollution-related disease. Limits on factory and vehicle emissions and on contaminated water reduce asthma, heart disease and infections, and removing lead from petrol lowered lead poisoning in children. Air pollution contributes to millions of early deaths worldwide, and cleaner air means fewer hospital admissions and longer lives. A city that bans the dirtiest vehicles from its centre, for example, may see fewer children treated for breathing problems within a few years. Safe water laws similarly prevent outbreaks of disease such as cholera, which spread quickly when drinking water is contaminated.

Furthermore, environmental laws prevent long-term harm that is hard to reverse. Controls on dangerous chemicals and waste protect farmland, rivers and food supplies, and the healthcare savings can outweigh the costs of compliance. However, the benefits are not automatic. Laws that are not enforced do little, and strict rules can raise costs for businesses and consumers, which may cause resistance. Health also depends on many other factors, such as diet, exercise, income and access to doctors, so environmental laws are only one part of the picture. They should be combined with support for industries that need to adapt.

In conclusion, stricter environmental laws improve public health to a large extent, because they reduce exposure to pollution, but their success depends on enforcement and on wider health policies.

plan.think: Mở bài nối môi trường với sức khoẻ (khói bụi, sông ô nhiễm, hoá chất trong đất) rồi largely agree + giới hạn (phụ thuộc thực thi và các yếu tố khác).

plan.step: 2. Lý do 1 — bảo vệ khỏi bệnh do ô nhiễm
plan.think: Giới hạn khí thải nhà máy, xe, nước nhiễm bẩn giảm hen, tim, nhiễm trùng; bỏ chì khỏi xăng giảm ngộ độc chì ở trẻ; ô nhiễm không khí gây hàng triệu cái chết sớm; luật nước an toàn ngăn dịch tả. Ví dụ thành phố cấm xe bẩn nhất vào trung tâm.

plan.step: 3. Lý do 2 — ngăn tác hại dài hạn + giới hạn
plan.think: Kiểm soát hoá chất nguy hiểm và chất thải bảo vệ đất, sông, thực phẩm; tiết kiệm y tế có thể lớn hơn chi phí tuân thủ. Giới hạn: luật không thực thi ít tác dụng; quy định nghiêm có thể làm tăng chi phí doanh nghiệp và người tiêu dùng; sức khoẻ còn phụ thuộc ăn uống, vận động, thu nhập, tiếp cận bác sĩ; hỗ trợ ngành cần thích ứng.
Cải thiện ở mức độ lớn, thành công phụ thuộc thực thi và chính sách y tế rộng hơn.
